summary: Defines the Autonomic Control Plane (ACP), a self-managing, largely configuration-independent control plane intended for autonomic functions. It supplies the addressing and routing those functions need to communicate, and can also serve as a stable management channel.

plainLanguage.summary: The Autonomic Control Plane is a private network that network devices build for themselves, on top of the same cables they already use. Each device finds its neighbours, opens an encrypted tunnel to each of them, gives itself an address in that private network, and learns routes across it. Because the tunnels do not depend on the normal forwarding tables, a device can still be reached and repaired even when the network around it is misconfigured.

subtitle: A self-building, encrypted IPv6 overlay that lets network devices reach each other even when the network is misconfigured.

tldr.problem: Network management and control traffic normally rides on the same network it manages. When an operator misconfigures routing, addressing or a firewall, the tools used to fix it often stop working too, because they depend on the paths that were just broken.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8994 defines a control plane that a node builds by itself: it discovers neighbours over link-local IPv6, sets up encrypted hop-by-hop tunnels to them, assigns itself an address inside that overlay, and runs a routing protocol inside it. The only thing it needs to start is its own certificate.
tldr.outcome: Management and control traffic survives data-plane misconfiguration, miswiring and network partitions, and the overlay costs no extra cabling because it runs in band. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8994 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2021, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the Autonomic Control Plane on top of GRASP, described in RFC 8990, and is used by the zero-touch enrolment work in RFC 8995.

sections.title: Why a Separate Control Plane
sections.content:
Autonomic Networking is a concept of self-management: autonomic functions self-configure, and negotiate parameters and settings across the network. Autonomic functions need an autonomically built communications infrastructure, which needs to be secure, resilient, and reusable by all autonomic functions. The document RFC 7575, which defines the fundamental ideas and design goals of Autonomic Networking, introduces that infrastructure and calls it the Autonomic Control Plane.

Today, the OAM and control plane of IP networks is what is typically called in-band management and signalling: its management and control protocol traffic depends on the routing and forwarding tables, security, policy, QoS, and potentially other configuration that first has to be established through the very same management and control protocols. Misconfigurations, including unexpected side effects or mutual dependencies, can disrupt OAM and control operations, and especially disrupt remote management access to the affected node itself, and potentially disrupt access to a much larger number of nodes for which the affected node is on the network path. The document cites an example from a regulatory filing in which engineers who had misdiagnosed a problem were unable to resolve it by restoring the link, because the network management tools required to do so remotely relied on the same paths they had just disabled.

Traditionally, physically separate, so-called out-of-band management networks have been used to avoid these problems, or at least to allow recovery from them. In the worst case, personnel are sent on site to access devices through out-of-band management ports, also called craft ports, serial consoles, or management Ethernet ports. Both options are expensive. In increasingly automated networks, both centralized management systems and distributed autonomic service agents require a control plane that is independent of the configuration of the network they manage, to avoid impacting their own operations through the configuration actions they take.

The document therefore describes a modular design for a self-forming, self-managing and self-protecting ACP, which is a virtual out-of-band network designed to be as independent as possible of configuration, addressing, and routing, while still operating in band on the same physical network it is controlling and managing. The design is intended to combine as well as possible the resilience of out-of-band management networks with the low cost of traditional IP in-band network management.

The ACP serves several purposes simultaneously. Autonomic functions communicate over it, so it directly supports Autonomic Networking functions; GRASP runs securely inside the ACP and depends on it as its security and transport substrate. A controller or network management system can use it to securely bootstrap network devices in remote locations, even if the network in between is not yet configured. And an operator can use it to reach remote devices with protocols such as SSH or NETCONF, even if the network is misconfigured or unconfigured.

The document notes the self-healing and self-protecting properties that follow. New neighbours automatically join the ACP after validation and become reachable by their unique address across it. When the topology changes, the routing protocol inside the ACP adapts and keeps providing reachability. The ACP tracks the validity of peer certificates and tears down secure channels when a peer certificate has expired, which removes invalid peers at a speed comparable to a certificate revocation check. Practically all ACP operations are link local, so a network partition has no impact on them, and the routing protocol inside each part of the ACP leads to two working, although partitioned, ACPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is a circular one: the tools that fix the network need the network to work. The ACP is built so that it does not need the normal forwarding tables, so a mistake in those tables cannot take the management channel down with it. It is a private overlay, but it runs over the cabling that is already there, so it costs far less than a separate management network.

sections.title: How the ACP Builds Itself
sections.content:
When a node has an ACP certificate and is enabled to bring up the ACP, it creates its ACP without any configuration, in the following steps.

First, the node creates a VRF instance, or a similar virtual context, for the ACP. Second, it assigns its ULA IPv6 address or prefix, which is learned from the acp-node-name of its ACP certificate, to an ACP loopback interface and connects that interface to the ACP VRF. Third, it establishes a list of candidate peer adjacencies and candidate channel types to try, which is automatic for all candidate link-local adjacencies across all native interfaces; if a candidate peer is discovered via multiple interfaces, this results in one adjacency per interface. Fourth, for each entry in the candidate adjacency list, the node negotiates a secure tunnel using the candidate channel types. Fifth, the node authenticates the peer node during secure channel setup and authorizes it to become part of the ACP. Sixth, unsuccessful authentication of a candidate peer results in throttled connection retries for as long as the candidate peer is discoverable. Seventh, each successfully established secure channel is mapped to an ACP virtual interface, which is placed into the ACP VRF. Eighth, each node runs a lightweight routing protocol to announce reachability of its ACP loopback address or prefix across the ACP.

This completes the creation of the ACP with hop-by-hop secure tunnels, auto-addressing, and auto-routing, and the node is now an ACP node with a running ACP. None of those operations, except the explicitly configured ones, is reflected in the configuration of the node. Non-ACP network management systems or SDN controllers have to be explicitly configured for connection to the ACP, and additional candidate peer adjacencies for ACP connections across non-ACP Layer 3 clouds require explicit configuration.

The resulting overlay network is normally based exclusively on hop-by-hop tunnels, because the addressing used on links is IPv6 link-local addressing, which does not require any prior setup. In this way the ACP can be built even if there is no configuration on the node, or if the data plane has issues such as addressing or routing problems.

The ACP is therefore automatically self-creating, which makes it largely indestructible against most changes to the data plane, including misconfigurations of routing, addressing, NAT, firewall, or any other traffic policy filters that would inadvertently also affect the management plane traffic, such as the operator command-line interface session through which the configuration changes are executed. Physical misconfiguration of wiring between ACP nodes will also not break the ACP: as long as there is a transitive physical path between ACP nodes, the ACP should be able to recover, given that it automatically operates across all interfaces of the ACP nodes and automatically determines paths between them. Attacks against the network via incorrect routing or addressing information for the data plane will not impact the ACP.
sections.plainLanguage: Nine steps, none of which the operator performs. The node makes a private routing table, gives itself an address, finds its neighbours, opens a tunnel to each, checks each neighbour's certificate, and then runs a routing protocol inside the tunnels. The address it uses comes out of its own certificate, and the addresses on the links are link-local, so no configuration has to be in place first.

sections.title: The ACP Certificate, Domain and Node Name
sections.content:
The ACP relies on group security. An ACP domain is a group of nodes that trust each other to take part in ACP operations such as creating secure channels in an autonomous, peer-to-peer fashion between domain members using protocols such as IPsec. To authenticate and authorize another member, each node requires keying material: an ACP node must have an LDevID certificate and information about one or more trust anchors, as required for the ACP domain membership check. Manual keying via shared secrets is not usable for a domain, because it would require a single shared secret across all current and future members to meet the expectation of autonomous, peer-to-peer establishment of secure channels between any two of them. Asymmetric keying material without certificates does not provide a mechanism to authenticate domain membership in an autonomous, peer-to-peer fashion. The LDevID certificate is henceforth called the ACP certificate, and the trust anchor is the CA root certificate of the domain.

ACP certificates must be compliant X.509 v3 certificates. Nodes must support handling ACP certificates, trust anchor certificates and certificate chain certificates with RSA public keys and with elliptic curve public keys. They must not support certificates with RSA public keys of less than a 2048-bit modulus or curves with group order of less than 256 bits. They must support certificates with RSA public keys with a 2048-bit modulus, and ECDSA certificates using the NIST P-256 curve, and should support P-384 and P-521. The reason is that as of 2020 RSA is still more widely used than elliptic curve, while ECC offers equivalent security at logarithmically shorter key lengths, which benefits constrained networks.

The ACP node name. The identity of a node in the ACP is carried in a field called the acp-node-name, defined by this ABNF: a local part, an at sign, and an acp-domain-name. The local part is an optional acp-address of 32 hexadecimal digits or the single character zero, optionally followed by a plus sign and a routing subdomain, and optionally further plus-separated extensions. The acp-domain-name is a domain name. As an example, an ACP address of fd89:b714:f3db:0:200:0:6400:0000, an ACP domain name of acp.example.com and an rsub extension of area51.research give the node name fd89b714f3db00000200000064000000+area51.research@acp.example.com, and the routing subdomain area51.research.acp.example.com.

The certificate must carry this information in an otherName field in the X.509 Subject Alternative Name extension. Nodes must be able to receive their ACP address through the domain certificate, in which case their own certificate must have a 32-hex-digit acp-address field; the field is case insensitive, and encoding it in lowercase is recommended. Nodes must also be able to authenticate nodes as domain members or as secure channel peers when they have a zero-value acp-address field, and as domain members when the field is omitted entirely.

The acp-domain-name indicates the domain across which nodes authenticate and authorize each other. It should be the fully qualified domain name of an Internet domain owned by the network administration of the ACP and ideally reserved for the ACP alone, serving as a name that is ideally globally unique. Using different domain names, operators can distinguish multiple ACPs even when using the same trust anchor. The routing subdomain allows a single domain to employ multiple /48 prefixes. The optional extensions field is for future standardized extensions and must be ignored if present and not understood.
sections.plainLanguage: Every node carries a certificate that says who it is and which control plane it belongs to. The name in the certificate has two parts: a unique address for the node and the name of the domain. Because the address is inside the certificate, a node can work out its own control-plane address without asking anybody, which is what makes the whole thing self-starting.

sections.title: Discovery and Secure Channels
sections.content:
Discovery Unsolicited Link-Local GRASP, known as DULL GRASP, is a limited subset of GRASP intended to operate across an insecure link-local scope. The ACP uses one instance of DULL GRASP for every Layer 2 interface of the node, to discover candidate ACP neighbours that are link-level adjacent. Native interfaces should be initialized automatically to a state in which ACP discovery can be performed, and any native interface with ACP neighbours can then be brought into the ACP even if the interface is otherwise unconfigured. Reception of packets on such otherwise unconfigured interfaces must be limited so that at first only SLAAC and DULL GRASP work, and then only the ACP secure channel setup packets, but not any other unnecessary traffic.

The use of the IPv6 link-local multicast address implies the need for MLDv2 to announce the desire to receive packets for that address, otherwise DULL GRASP could fail in the presence of switches that do not forward it. ACP discovery should not be enabled by default on non-native interfaces, and in particular must not run inside the ACP across ACP virtual interfaces.

An ACP node announces itself to potential peers using the AN_ACP objective, a synchronization objective intended to be flooded on a single link using the GRASP Flood Synchronization message. A locator consisting of a specific link-local IP address, IP protocol number and port number is distributed with the flooded objective. The method name in the objective value is a string indicating the protocol available at the locator, for example IKEv2 for an IPsec secure channel or DTLS. The recommended period of sending the objective is 60 seconds, and the indicated time to live of 210000 msec means the objective would be cached by nodes even when two out of three messages are dropped in transit. The loop count is fixed at 1 since this is a link-local operation, and the originator must be the IPv6 link-local address of the sending node on that interface.

Every ACP node maintains an adjacency table, which holds at a minimum the node identifier, the interface on which the neighbour was discovered, the link-local IPv6 address of the neighbour on that interface, and the neighbour's certificate including its acp-node-name. The table is used to decide to which neighbour a connection is established. It may hold information about the validity and trust of the neighbour's certificate, but the domain membership check against the peer must always follow.

Secure channels. Due to channel selection, the ACP can support an evolving set of security association protocols and does not require support for a single network-wide mandatory-to-implement protocol. Nodes only need to implement the protocols required to interoperate with their candidate peers. The degree of security required on every hop needs to be consistent across the network, so that there is no designated weakest link, because a compromised link can be used to send and receive packets across the whole ACP network.

The authentication of peers in any security association protocol must use the ACP certificate. Because auto-discovery of candidate neighbours via GRASP does not communicate the neighbour's certificate, and nodes may not yet have any other network connectivity to retrieve certificates, any security association protocol must use a mechanism to communicate the certificate directly rather than relying on a referential mechanism such as communicating only a hash or a URL. A security association protocol must use forward secrecy. Because the ACP payload of legacy protocol payloads inside the ACP and hop-by-hop flooded GRASP information is unencrypted, the secure channel protocol requires confidentiality, using symmetric encryption of at least 256-bit key strength such as AES-256, and there must be no support for null encryption. A secure channel must be terminated immediately when the lifetime of any certificate in the chain used to authenticate the neighbour expires or becomes revoked, which may not be standard behaviour in the secure channel protocols themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Discovery is a small flood on the local link: each node shouts that it is here and which secure channels it can speak. The certificate is then exchanged as part of setting up the tunnel itself, not fetched by reference, because there may be no other way to reach a certificate server. The tunnel must be encrypted, must give forward secrecy, and must be torn down the moment a certificate expires.

sections.title: Addressing inside the ACP
sections.content:
The secure channels typically only establish communication between two adjacent nodes, so for communication to happen across multiple hops the Autonomic Control Plane requires network-wide valid addresses and routing. Each ACP node creates a loopback interface with an ACP network-wide unique address or prefix inside the ACP context. With the algorithm used here, all ACP nodes in the same routing subdomain have the same /48 unique local address prefix, and unique local address Global IDs from different domains are unlikely to clash, so two ACP networks can be merged as long as policy allows it. Links inside the ACP only use link-local IPv6 addressing, so each node's ACP requires only one routable address prefix.

The fundamental concepts are these. Autonomic addresses are used exclusively for self-management functions inside a trusted domain, and are not used for user traffic; communication with entities outside the trusted domain uses another address space, called the data plane in this document. The autonomic address space is used separately from the user address space and other address realms, which supports the robustness requirement. Only ACP loopback interfaces carry routable addresses; all other interfaces, called ACP virtual interfaces, only use IPv6 link-local addresses. Unique local addresses are used for the loopback interfaces, with the L bit set to 1 as defined in RFC 4193, and the random hash for ACP loopback addresses uses the definition in this document rather than the one in RFC 4193. The addresses do not provide access to the Internet. Addresses in the ACP are permanent and do not support temporary addresses, and they are not considered sensitive on privacy grounds, because ACP nodes are not expected to be end-user hosts and all ACP nodes are in one administrative domain.

The ACP addressing base scheme is 128 bits wide. The first 48 bits follow the unique local address scheme: an fd marker identifying a locally defined address, then a 40-bit Global ID, then a 2-bit Type field, then 78 bits for the sub-scheme. The 40-bit Global ID is the first 40 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the routing subdomain from the same acp-node-name. In the example given earlier, the routing subdomain is area51.research.acp.example.com and the Global ID is 89b714f3db. When creating a new routing subdomain for an existing network, it must be ensured that the rsub is selected so that the resulting hash does not collide with the hash of any pre-existing routing subdomain, so that addresses created by registrars for different routing subdomains do not collide with each other.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node gets one address that is routable inside the control plane, on a loopback interface, and uses link-local addresses everywhere else. The prefix is derived by hashing the routing subdomain, so two nodes in the same subdomain share a /48 prefix and two different subdomains are very unlikely to collide.

sections.title: Routing in the ACP
sections.content:
Once unique local addresses are set up, all autonomic entities should run a routing protocol within the ACP context. This routing protocol distributes the addresses for reachability. The use of the ACP-specific context eliminates the probable clash with data plane routing tables and also secures the ACP from interference from configuration mismatch or incorrect routing updates. The establishment of the routing plane and its parameters is automatic and strictly within the confines of the ACP, so no explicit configuration is required. All routing updates are automatically secured in transit, as the channels of the ACP are encrypted, and this routing runs only inside the ACP.

The routing protocol inside the ACP is RPL, the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks. RPL was chosen because it requires a smaller routing table footprint in large networks compared to other routing protocols with an autonomically configured single area, and because the deployment experience of large-scale Internet of Things networks serves as the basis for wide deployment experience with RPL. The profile chosen for RPL in the ACP does not leverage any RPL-specific forwarding plane features, meaning it avoids the IPv6 extension headers, which makes it a pure control plane software requirement.

RPL adjacencies are set up across all ACP channels in the same domain, including all of its routing subdomains. The profile that ACP nodes need to support by default does not use RPL Packet Information for better compatibility with accelerated hardware forwarding planes, which most often do not support the hop-by-hop headers used for it, and to avoid the overhead of that header on the wire and the cost of adding and removing it.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the overlay, nodes run RPL, the routing protocol designed for small devices, because it keeps the routing tables small. The RPL-specific headers that ordinary devices would need are left out, so this is a control-plane-only requirement and the normal forwarding path of the network is untouched.

sections.title: Connecting Non-ACP Components and Networks
sections.content:
The document explains how non-ACP nodes and networks can be integrated. The ACP Connect mechanism gives a controller, a network management system, or a piece of software on a non-ACP node a way to reach the ACP. A combined ACP and data plane interface lets the two coexist, with a VRF select mechanism to move between them. GRASP is used for the discovery of the peer on the other side.

Connecting ACP islands over non-ACP Layer 3 networks is also covered. A configured remote ACP neighbour is reached over an existing network connection, while a tunneled remote ACP neighbour is reached over a tunnel. Either way, the remote node is treated as a candidate peer, and the same certificate checks and secure channel setup apply as for a link-local neighbour.
sections.plainLanguage: Not everything in a network can be an ACP node. The document gives two ways to bridge the gap: a controller or management system that is not ACP-aware can be given a way into the ACP, and an ACP node on one side of an ordinary IP network can be treated as a candidate peer of one on the other side, whether over an existing connection or a tunnel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A set of ACP nodes with ACP certificates for the same domain and with ACP functionality enabled is automatically self-building: the ACP is established between neighbouring nodes, and it is also self-protecting, because the ACP secure channels are authenticated and encrypted. No configuration is required for this. The self-protecting property does not include workarounds for non-autonomic components.

The security of the ACP depends on a number of other factors. The use of domain certificates depends on a valid supporting public key infrastructure, and if the chain of trust of that infrastructure is compromised, the security of the ACP is compromised as well. ACP nodes receive their certificates from ACP registrars, which are security-critical dependencies: a malicious registrar can enroll malicious nodes into an ACP network, if the CA delegates that policy to it, or break ACP routing, for example by assigning duplicate ACP addresses to nodes through their certificates. Every ACP registrar and EST server is a security-critical entity and needs to be hardened against attacks, much like a CA and its protocols.

ACP nodes that are also ANI nodes rely on BRSKI as the protocol for ACP registrars, so the security considerations of BRSKI apply to them. BRSKI and other registrar protocol options require nodes to have an X.509 v3 based IDevID, which is an option for registrars to securely identify candidate nodes that should be enrolled. For an IDevID to securely identify the node to which it is assigned, the node needs hardware support such as a Trusted Platform Module to protect against extraction or cloning of the private key, and infrastructure that prohibits the execution of unauthenticated software to protect against malicious use of the IDevID. The ACP certificate should equally be protected from extraction or abuse by the same infrastructure.

Because ACP secure channels can be long lived while the certificates used may be short lived, secure channels have to be terminated when peer certificates expire. Where the ACP operates on what is effectively a large bridge domain, the ACP is subject to a much higher likelihood of attacks by other nodes stealing Layer 2 addresses than in the routed case, especially when the bridged network includes untrusted devices such as hosts. Layer 2 and Layer 3 devices often already have some form of port security, relying on Neighbor Discovery Protocol or DHCP learning to bind a port to a MAC address and IPv6 address, and blocking source addresses from the wrong ports. That function needs to be enabled to prohibit denial-of-service attacks and specifically to protect the ACP, and the DULL GRASP instance needs to ensure that the IPv6 address in the locator option matches the source IPv6 address of the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The overlay protects itself, but it rests on three things outside its own control: a trustworthy certificate authority, trustworthy registrars that enrol nodes, and a device whose own identity key cannot be copied. The document also warns that running the ACP over a flat Layer 2 network makes address-stealing attacks easier, so port security should be switched on.

items.text: An operator can reach remote devices with SSH or NETCONF even if the network is misconfigured or unconfigured.
